WindDancer: Understanding Acoustic Sensing under Ambient Airflow

a general framework that explains how ambient airflow impacts a range of existing acoustic sensing systems
Kuang Yuan1 · Dong Li2 · Hao Zhou3 · Zhehao Li4 · Lili Qiu5 · Swarun Kumar1 · Jie Xiong6

What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

Acoustic sensing in rooms with fans and air conditioners

Imagine a meeting room with a fan or the air conditioning on: a smart speaker on the table keeps sensing by sound.

the speed of sound · still air and a fan

It shows The speed of sound, chirp by chirp: flat in still air, jumping at random when a fan blows across the path.

How to read it Time runs to the right and the line is the speed in m/s: its jumps are a few cm/s, between every two chirps.

drag to turn the space
Office · Meeting room · Sensing World ›
Motivation

Indoor airflow is common, and acoustic sensing assumes still air

  1. 1fans and air conditioners are widely used
  2. 2prior systems employed the background subtraction method
  3. 3prior systems extracted the phase at the target range bin
  4. 4prior solutions have mitigated wind noise on voice
  5. 5Existing acoustic sensing systems assume the medium is stable
background subtraction

It shows Two chirps' range profiles and their difference: the static peaks cancel and only the moving target is left.

How to read it Each bump is an echo at a distance: grey is chirp n−1, ink is chirp n, and the accent line is their difference.

static vector removal

It shows The target's bin on the I-Q plane: a fixed arrow to the circle's centre (static) plus a turning arrow (the target).

How to read it The tip runs round the circle as the target moves; removing the centre leaves the turn, which gives the displacement.

wind-noise reduction

It shows A voice recording with wind noise, and the same voice after the noise is filtered: wind treated as noise on audible sound.

How to read it The top trace is speech with gusts of wind noise, and the bottom one is the same speech after the noise is filtered.

State of the art

Real-world factors were studied, but not airflow

  1. 1Recent papers identify real-world factors such as device mobility, multi-target interference, and audible leakage
  2. 2The impact of airflow on sound wave propagation, and consequently on acoustic sensing, remains relatively underexplored
  3. 3these studies did not examine how measured airflow and turbulence impact acoustic sensing

It shows Real-world factors acoustic sensing had studied, and the one left out: airflow.

How to read it Each row is a factor and a filled mark means earlier papers handled it, so the empty airflow row is the gap WindDancer fills.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Chirp (FMCW)01

a sine wave whose frequency sweeps linearly over time

Range bin02

separate the reflections from different distances into various range bins

Background subtraction03

we calculate the difference of CFRs between two consecutive chirp signals

Static vector04

a summation of a constant vector (from static reflectors) and a dynamic vector (from the moving target)

a chirp: frequency over time

It shows The chirp's frequency rises from 18 to 22 kHz in 50 ms, then starts again.

How to read it Time runs to the right and frequency up, and the echo is the same line shifted later by the trip's time.

echo strength by range bin

It shows The echo's strength at each distance: one bump for each thing that reflects the chirp.

How to read it Each bar is a 4.29 cm range bin, and the target and each box make a bump at their own distance.

Core idea

Turbulence makes static echoes change from chirp to chirp

  1. 1airflow does not degrade acoustic sensing performance by directly causing calculation errors
  2. 2turbulence in the air introduces abrupt and random fluctuations in the sound speed
  3. 3the CFRs from static objects can no longer be treated as constant over time
measured speed of sound · with and without wind

It shows The speed of sound measured between two microphones 1 m apart: flat in still air, jumping when a fan blows (the paper's Fig. 5).

How to read it Time runs to the right over 60 s, grey with no wind and the accent line with wind, whose jumps are a few cm/s.

Core idea · what to observe

With wind, static reflectors appear in the subtracted range map

some peaks appear at distances where no moving objects are present

  1. Still air: one bright row, the target
  2. Fan on: the sound speed jumps each chirp
  3. Rows light up at the boxes, where nothing moves
  4. The peak lands on a box: a range error
Speed of sound now –
Range error, last 4 s –
range map after subtraction

It shows Each bin's strength after one chirp is taken from the next: in still air only the target shows, with wind the reflectors light up too.

How to read it Time runs left to right over 6 s and range goes up; brighter is stronger, and the dots are the peak picked.

speed of sound, m/s

It shows The speed of sound on the path, one value a chirp: the fan makes it jump at random by a few cm/s.

How to read it The dashed line is still air at 343 m/s; the solid line is the speed of each chirp.

The real system

Airflow raises sensing errors, and two fixes reduce them

92%
more object-detection error with a regular fan
172%
more fine-grained tracking error with a regular fan
67.3%
mean ranging error: 11.0 → 3.6 cm
52.5%
mean tracking error: 13.9 → 6.6 %

Our evaluation results show that the algorithms achieve 67.3% and 52.5% performance improvements in coarse-grained and fine-grained sensing respectivelyOur comparison: 3.6 cm is about two fingers wide, still above the 1.8 cm with no wind. Ranging: averaged over ten settings with different reflectors and wind (§7.1). Tracking: a board moved 1 cm, 150 ms chirps, reflectors 0.8–1.2 m (§7.2).

Measured in the paper, §1, §7.1, §7.2
the paper's numbers · raw and with WindDancer

It shows The errors the paper measured without and with its two fixes: both drop by more than half, yet stay above still air.

How to read it Left: the ranging error in cm; right: the tracking error in % of the move; dashed: the error with no wind.

Challenge 1 · coarse-grained ranging

Static echoes survive background subtraction under airflow

the subtraction of two consecutive CFR vectors would not be a zero vector due to the fluctuations of the speed of sound

the stronger reflector generates considerably more interference than the weaker one

  1. New: a fan beside the signal path
  2. Each box's echo no longer cancels
  3. The peak jumps to a box: the range is wrong
  4. Your turn Drag the target
Range error, last 4 s –
range map after subtraction

It shows With the fan on, the two still boxes leave bright rows after subtraction, the stronger one more, so the peak often lands on a box.

How to read it Time runs left to right over 6 s and range goes up; brighter is stronger, and the dots are the peak picked.

where wind breaks the pipeline

It shows The usual sensing steps, from the chirp to the range and to the motion: the two marked steps fail when the air moves.

How to read it Follow the arrows; marked boxes break under airflow, and the peak box shows the range picked now, marked when it is wrong.

speed of sound, m/s

It shows The speed of sound on the path, one value a chirp: the fan makes it jump at random by a few cm/s.

How to read it The dashed line is still air at 343 m/s; the solid line is the speed of each chirp.

Solution 1 · Spectral thresholding

Spectral thresholding masks range bins that hold only still things

the CFR from static reflectors exhibits a stable spectral pattern, whereas the CFR from moving objects shows greater variationwe propose to mask out the CFR if the V M is lower than a threshold, before the final range bin estimation

  1. New: each bin is checked
  2. Still bins: one 0 Hz peak; the target: many
  3. V under the threshold: masked
  4. The peak comes from the rest
  5. Your turn Off and on: compare

On average, the original pipeline has a ranging error of 11.0 cm, while our algorithm reduces the mean error to 3.6 cmthe error is still slightly higher than the error without wind (1.8 cm)

Range error, last 4 s –
range map, raw and masked

It shows The raw map beside the masked one over the same 4 s: masking takes out the flat bins, so the peak stays on the target.

How to read it Time runs left to right and range goes up; brighter is stronger, grey cells are masked, and the dots are the peak picked.

spectrum, last 10 s

It shows The box's spectrum is one 0 Hz peak on a flat floor that the fan raises (dashed: the same box without the fan; thin: the box alone in a weaker and a stronger wind, as in Fig. 14(a)); the target's move gives many peaks and valleys. The spectra are averaged over 3 s parts. V, over the paper's 0.5 s, measures that spread.

How to read it Frequency runs left to right from -5 to 5 Hz, in dB under each line's own peak; beside each line, its V against the threshold, and whether it is masked.

Challenge 2 · fine-grained tracking

The static vector drifts, so the I-Q circle loses its centre

the static I-Q vector from the static reflector is no longer a constant and starts shifting over time

the I-Q vector from target movements rotates more randomly without a fixed central point

  1. New: a box in the target's range bin
  2. With wind, the circle's centre wanders
  3. The displacement drifts off the true one
  4. Your turn Drag the target
Error, % of the move –
CFR at the target's bin

It shows The signal at the target's range bin: the target draws a circle, but its centre, the still part, shifts as the wind changes c.

How to read it The trail is the last 2 s on the I-Q plane; the cross is the circle's fitted centre.

the target's move, mm

It shows The target's move read from the phase against its true 1 cm move: the shifting centre bends the reading and makes it drift.

How to read it Time runs left to right over 6 s; dashed is the true move, solid is the reading, both in mm.

Solution 2 · VMD separation

VMD separates the target's signal from the still reflectors

we empirically find that the last IMF is always a component with a dominant spectral peak at 0 Hz, associated with the static reflectorswe retain the first N − 1 IMFs and add them up to perform signal reconstruction

  1. New: VMD splits the signal
  2. Last IMF, a 0 Hz peak: still things
  3. The rest added: the target
  4. Its phase follows the move: the error drops
  5. Your turn Off and on: compare

The error on average is reduced from 13.9% to 6.6%the error after applying our algorithm is slightly higher compared to the performance under wind-free conditions

Error, % of the move –
the target bin's spectrum

It shows The raw spectrum and the two parts VMD finds: the still part holds the 0 Hz peak, the target's part the peaks beside it.

How to read it Frequency runs left to right with 0 Hz in the middle, in dB; dashed is the raw signal; VMD off, it alone.

target's part, I-Q

It shows With VMD on, the target's part alone: a circle round zero, so its phase gives the move.

How to read it The last 3 s; at the paper's 150 ms chirps a circle has few points; VMD off, the raw signal and its centre.

target's move, mm

It shows The raw reading bends off the true 1 cm move; the reading after VMD follows it more closely. The readout gives this run's error, raw then after VMD.

How to read it Time runs left to right, in mm; dashed is the true move; with VMD on, every line is 6 s late, as VMD reads.

Ranging a moving board beside a fan

Question How close is our simulation to the paper's own tests?We run each test of the paper through our chain and set our points beside the paper's. The paper fits its AR air model for each set-up, and it does not give the real reflectors' strengths: ours are assumed.

Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question What does each of the two modules add under a fan?Spectral thresholding lowers the range error (§7.1). VMD lowers the tracking error (§7.2). Both leave it a little above the error in still air. Each one is switched off here, in the air of Fig. 8's worst place (assumed).

Why it matters Each module lowers one of the two errors that airflow adds, so each one off should bring its own error back up.The range test: the target at 1 m, moving 1 cm (assumed), still objects at about 1.2 and 1.9 m as in Fig. 15(a). The tracking test: 150 ms chirps, still objects at 1.0 and 1.1 m, 10 dB stronger than the target (assumed).

You change
the two modules, one off at a time
  1. 1Your turn PressWithout it the echoes of still things can make the tallest peak, so the range jumps to them.
  2. 2Your turn PressWithout it the static part, which wobbles with the air, stays in the target's signal and bends the move.
  3. 3Your turn PressWith two IMFs only the first one is kept as the target's. The paper finds the error then higher than with no VMD at all.
  4. 4Your turn PressBoth modules on, threshold 0.1 and four IMFs: WindDancer as the paper runs it.
More controls

Tracking error, 1 cm move paper 6.6 %–

The tracking error is the move's peak-to-peak error over the 1 cm move.we empirically set the threshold as 0.1 and we use a 0.5 s time window to segment the signal and calculate the spectral variation the significant drift in the waveform is effectively removed When the number of IMFs is two (i.e. only use the first IMF as the target CFR), the error is even higher than the raw CFR When the number of IMFs is higher than 3, we obtain a consistently satisfactory performance for error mitigation our proposed spectral variation thresholding algorithm effectively reduces the mean error to 3.6 cm

Check the Paper · 3 of 3

Comparison with related work

Question Would a CW phase tracker such as LLAP do better under the same airflow?FMCW keeps only the echoes in the board's range bin. LLAP (MobiCom 2016) sends 16 steady tones, 350 Hz apart, and finds the static vector with its LEVD. It cannot sort echoes by range, so every static echo joins that vector.

Our findings regarding the speed of sound fluctuations and preliminary experiments suggest that similar airflow effects exist in other signal types, including CW signalsWindDancer studies FMCW only. This page models LLAP, a CW tracker it cites for removing the static vector (§3), under the same air.

Go Beyond the Paper · 1 of 3

Generalization study

Question Where does thresholding stop saving the range?The paper puts the target at 1 m, with σ up to 0.049 m/s and still objects up to +20 dB. Here the target goes from 0.3 to 2 m, σ to 0.08 m/s and the objects to +30 dB.

Why it matters The paper tests thresholding in its own set-ups only, so the model shows how far past them it still lowers the error.Thresholding hides a range bin whose spectrum stays flat over 0.5 s. Here the model is run with a farther target, stronger turbulence and louder still objects than the paper tried.

You change
the target's range, the air and the still objects
  1. 1Your turn Drag the board along the path.Each place on the path gets its own run of the model. The two still objects stay at 1.2 and 1.9 m (Fig. 15(a)'s places).
  2. 2Your turn PressTwice the paper's strongest bladeless fan: the speed of sound jumps twice as far from chirp to chirp.
  3. 3Your turn PressEach still object echoes 30 dB louder than the target, 10 dB past the paper's loudest test.
  4. 4Your turn PressBack to the start: the air of Fig. 8's worst place, still objects as loud as the target (assumed).

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which change of the air hurts the range, and which does not?Existing systems take the speed of sound as constant, about 343 m/s (§1), and so does the model's processing. Here the air is warmed, a heater or a humidifier stands in for the fan, and the turbulence is set by hand.

Why it matters The paper calls slow changes of temperature and humidity predictable, and the fast changes of airflow the harder problem.A fast jump of the speed between two chirps leaves a leftover echo at each still object. The paper's Eq. 9 says so: two echoes of one still object no longer cancel when the speed differs.

You change
the air: its temperature, the device, the turbulence
TemperatureComfort deviceTurbulence
  1. 1Your turn Warm the air to 40 °C.Sound travels at 331.3 + 0.606 T m/s (a textbook rule, assumed). The processing keeps the 343 m/s that existing systems assume (§1), so every range reads short in warm air. The fan is off here.
Range scale read –
Range error, fan off –

What you saw The paper measures the speed near a heater (Fig. 18), not ranging in warm air. At 40 °C the speed is 3.7 % above 343 m/s, less than one 4.29 cm range bin at 1 m.Generally, an acoustic wave travels faster in warmer and more humid air

  1. 1Your turn Pick the heater.Fig. 18 of the paper: near the heater the speed rises about 0.2 m/s over 100 s. Near the humidifier it stays flat, and near the fan it jumps. Try the humidifier next.

Go Beyond the Paper · 3 of 3

Device design

Question Where should the speaker and mic go, and how long a chirp?Each box echoes too. When the wind shifts the speed of sound, its echo no longer cancels. For fine tracking, a box in the board's own range bin hurts most (Fig. 12).

You change
the speaker & mic's place, the boxes, the chirp
You watch
the two errors
  1. 1Your turn Drag the speaker & mic to a new place.The board's range is its distance from the speaker & mic; the dashed ring marks its range bin.
  2. 2Your turn Drag a box onto the dashed ring.A box in the board's range bin mixes its echo with the board's; the paper shows this for fine tracking (Fig. 12).
  3. 3Your turn Set a longer chirp.Longer chirps put fewer samples on the I-Q circle, so fine tracking suffers (Fig. 13).
  4. 4Your turn PressBack to the start: the speaker & mic at the path's end (Fig. 7), the board at 1 m (§6), boxes at 0.8 m and 1.2 m (§7.2 places its reflectors 0.8 to 1.2 m away).
